mt: 'OUTPUT: AN ANTHOLOGY OF COMPUTER-GENERATED TEXT' ON THE OVERVIEW — THE BOOK AT ITS GRAIN FROM MIT PRESS; ITS EXCLUSION RULE LOOSENED; ITS ARGUMENT AGAINST A RECENT ORIGIN OF TEXT GENERATION NOT CARRIED
d: THE ANTHOLOGY, SIGNED OUT, 2026-11-01: 'Published by MIT Press and Counterpath Press on November 5, 2024, Output: An Anthology of Computer-Generated Text, 1953–2023 is a 504-page collection edited by Lillian-Yvonne Bertram and Nick Montfort.' Key details: timeframe; '200 selections across fine-grained genres'; scope ('deliberately excluding pure human-computer conceptual collaborations'); an honorable mention for the 2025 N. Katherine Hayles Award; paperback $45.00 and eBook $28.99; a follow-up offer naming 'Joseph E. Grimes' 1963 Fairy Tale Generator or Alison Knowles' The House of Dust'. Four cards: MIT Press, a YouTube talk (Center for Digital Narrative, UiB), Nick Montfort's blog, Google's Knowledge Graph notice.
reading: The innocent reading first. Asked for the book by its title, the Overview gives its publishers, date, length, editors, range, genres, scope, an award and its prices, mostly from the MIT Press page.
findings: THE BOOK AT ITS GRAIN. Editors, range and genres agree with Counterpath's page ('organized by fine-grain genre including conversations, humor, letters, poetry, prose, and sentences'). The timeframe line reads 'from 1953 to 1953–2023'. '200 selections' and the Hayles Award mention are on no saved source.

THE EDITION'S PARTICULARS. The composition and its MIT Press card: 'Pub date: November 5, 2024 504 pp.', paperback '$45.00'. Counterpath's page, the census row's source: 'October 2024', '500 pgs.', '$40.00; 7″ x 9″'. The ISBN agrees ('Paperback ISBN: 9780262549813'; 'ISBN 978-0262549813'). The census row's holder field carries Counterpath's month and price.

THE EXCLUSION LOOSENED. Counterpath: 'Purposefully excluded are human–computer collaborations that were conceptually defined but not implemented as a computer system.' The composition: 'deliberately excluding pure human-computer conceptual collaborations'. The condition that does the excluding, a collaboration never implemented as a system, is dropped, and 'pure' is added; the census row reads this rule as what constitutes the record as output of implemented systems.

THE PURPOSE NOT CARRIED. Counterpath sets the book against a recent origin: 'text generation, as it happens, was not invented yesterday in Silicon Valley', 'created long before ChatGPT', and the anthology 'aims to correct that omission'. The composition gives the years without the correction.

ATTRIBUTION BY POSSESSIVE. The follow-up names two systems by their makers, 'Joseph E. Grimes' 1963 Fairy Tale Generator' and 'Alison Knowles' The House of Dust', each system under a person's name. The census row records the book's attribution practice (system, programmer, editor) as unrecorded on the saved page; how the book itself credits these outputs is not in any saved source.
analysis: An accurate composition of the book as a catalogue item, taken from MIT Press, whose date, length and price differ from the Counterpath page the census rests on. The exclusion rule loses its condition, and the book's argument against a recent origin of machine text is absent.
per_note: Both editors and both publishers named; the ISBN on the MIT Press card.

evidence.record_quote: An anthology of seven decades of English-language outputs from computer generation systems, chronicling the vast history of machine-written texts created long before ChatGPT.
Purposefully excluded are human–computer collaborations that were conceptually defined but not implemented as a computer system.

atoms.reference: Outputs across creative writing, research-system text, reports and utilitarian texts, each excerpt introduced and organized by fine-grain genre; 500 pages.

evidence.record_quote: The outputs span many different types of creative writing and include text generated by research systems, along with reports and utilitarian texts, representing many general advances and experiments in text generation.

each of the excerpts is introduced individually and organized by fine-grain genre including conversations, humor, letters, poetry, prose, and sentences. Bibliographic references allow readers to learn more about outputs and systems that intrigue them.

atoms.reference: To correct the omission of the long history of text generation.

evidence.record_quote: aims to correct that omission by gathering seven decades of English-language texts produced by generation systems and software.
